video.title: How much faster can a quantum computer be? OpenAI’s fourth-power result
video.description: I compare how many times quantum and classical computers must look at the same data, then explain why four is the best possible power for total yes-or-no questions.

exposition.audience: General mathematical readers familiar with probability and linear algebra; Sections 1–6 form the main argument, with optional appendices
exposition.question: How much can a quantum algorithm save when both algorithms have to read the same hidden bits?
exposition.preview: Imagine a board with one winning column. A classical algorithm can spend almost all its queries finding the right square to inspect. A quantum algorithm can compare two columns cheaply before checking a short list of candidates. Follow a four-column example through both searches to see why the gap approaches a fourth power.

expert.question: What lets this construction pass the cubic separation from earlier cheat sheets?
expert.preview: The quantum saving comes from comparing candidates before paying to verify one. The classical obstruction is that a query to the planted cell must name an address formed from independent hard answers. Trace the weighted pivot law and the separate-cap prediction bound, then see where their exponents meet.

reconstruction.audience: Readers checking the full derivation or its formal statements
reconstruction.question: How do the detailed proofs and quantitative estimates fit together?
reconstruction.preview: Read the complete separation argument, the supporting quantum and classical proofs, and the Forrelation lower bound. Consult a particular derivation or follow the continuous proof; source correspondence explains where the argument and the Lean take different routes.

original.audience: Readers checking the result against OpenAI’s original paper
original.question: What does OpenAI’s original paper state and prove?
original.preview: Read the original wording, construction and proof in a source-preserving text edition, or open the published PDF. Editorial links connect its statements to the accompanying explanations and Lean.

semantic_probes.name: wrong_quantifier_order_changes_answer
semantic_probes.question: Could a different zero-query program be chosen after seeing each input?
semantic_probes.answer: If the algorithm may depend on the input, it can pick the correct constant answer and spend zero queries. One algorithm chosen in advance cannot compute the one-bit identity with zero queries.

semantic_probes.name: strict_threshold_mutant_rejects_mixture
semantic_probes.question: Does replacing success at least two thirds with strictly greater success change a boundary case?
semantic_probes.answer: On the all-false input the example algorithm for two-bit OR succeeds with probability exactly two thirds. Requiring strictly greater success rules out that algorithm.

semantic_probes.name: off_promise_false_changes_zero_query_answer
semantic_probes.question: Does assigning false outside the promise change the zero-query answer?
semantic_probes.answer: A constant answer works on the example’s promise. Assigning false outside that promise creates two different required labels and forces at least one query.

semantic_probes.name: absolute_high_changes_answer
semantic_probes.question: Would taking the absolute value on the high branch accept a negative instance?
semantic_probes.answer: The example has a large negative Forrelation value. The published promise leaves it undefined. Taking the absolute value on the high branch instead accepts it as true.

semantic_probes.name: comparison_has_witness
semantic_probes.question: Can an actual comparison satisfy all of these assumptions?
semantic_probes.answer: Two candidates with comparison weight one half in each direction satisfy the comparison assumptions. There is an actual instance to which the theorem applies.

semantic_probes.name: trueOnly_Q_eq_zero
semantic_probes.question: Can a quantum algorithm use zero queries when every promised input has label true?
semantic_probes.answer: Always answering true uses zero quantum queries and succeeds on every promised input of this example.

semantic_probes.name: orTwo_R_eq_one
semantic_probes.question: How many randomized queries does two-bit OR require with success at least two thirds?
semantic_probes.answer: One randomized query suffices for two-bit OR with the stated error bound. Zero queries cannot distinguish its two labels.

semantic_probes.name: negativePair_Phi
semantic_probes.question: Can the Forrelation value actually reach minus one on two explicit layers?
semantic_probes.answer: Yes. For the two explicit sign layers, the numerator is minus eight and the denominator is eight, giving a Forrelation value of minus one.
